Earlier, WhatsApp launched parent-managed accounts for preschoolers, and today it is extending parental supervision features to teen accounts, adding group activity alerts and additional restrictions on Meta AI. Details are as follows.

WhatsApp expands parental supervision options

WhatsApp previously announced several new features aimed at giving parents greater control over their preschool-aged children's accounts.

These features include letting parents decide who can contact the account, which groups the account can join, viewing message requests from unknown contacts, and managing the account's privacy settings; all changes are protected by a password set by the parent.

A few weeks ago, WhatsApp further expanded this feature on iOS, adding a dedicated "Parental Supervision" section within the Settings app, making it easier for parents to find and configure managed accounts.

Today, WhatsApp is once again expanding the related supervision features—this time extending the applicable audience from preschoolers to teens—giving parents clearer insight into their children's group activity, while also having a greater say in how their children use Channels, Status updates, and interact with Meta AI.

After the update, parents can now receive notifications when their child joins or leaves a group, as well as alerts when the number of members in a group their child has already joined "increases significantly." Parents can also choose how their children use Channels, which Status updates they can view, and who can see their children's own Status updates.

As for Meta AI, parents can now choose between the standard experience designed for users aged 13 and above, and the stricter "Limited Content" option, depending on what they consider appropriate for their child.

According to WhatsApp, the "Limited Content" setting will further restrict the topics teens can discuss with Meta AI; at the same time, Meta AI features that rely on Private Processing technology will be unavailable when this setting is enabled.

WhatsApp once again emphasised that these parental supervision features do not allow parents to access the actual content of their children's messages or calls, which remain protected by end-to-end encryption.
